reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Characterised by an irresistible urge to move the legs, usually with uncomfortable sensations, that is partly or wholly relieved by movement
Symptoms worsen at rest and in the evening or night, disrupting sleep onset and contributing to daytime fatigue
Most patients also have periodic limb movements of sleep, which can be documented on polysomnography
Iron deficiency is a key and treatable contributor, so serum ferritin and transferrin saturation should be checked even when the haemoglobin is normal
Common secondary associations include pregnancy, chronic kidney disease and uraemia, and peripheral neuropathy
Certain drugs, including many antidepressants, antihistamines, and dopamine antagonists, can precipitate or aggravate symptoms
Treatment principles include iron repletion when stores are low, alpha-2-delta ligands, and dopaminergic agents, with attention to non-pharmacological measures
Long-term dopamine agonist use can lead to augmentation, a worsening and earlier onset of symptoms that requires careful management
reference.pathophysiology: Restless legs syndrome is a sensorimotor disorder linked to dysfunction of central dopaminergic transmission and to abnormal brain iron handling, since iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis. Reduced iron availability within the central nervous system, even with normal peripheral stores, is thought to impair dopaminergic signalling in circuits including the spinal cord and diencephalon. There is a strong genetic contribution, and it may be primary or secondary to iron deficiency, uraemia, pregnancy, or neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral vascular disease and venous insufficiency
Positional discomfort and habitual foot tapping
Periodic limb movement disorder without the sensory urge
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to assess iron status
Renal function tests to identify uraemia
Blood glucose and evaluation for peripheral neuropathy where clinically suspected
Review of medications that may provoke symptoms
Polysomnography in selected cases, particularly to document periodic limb movements or exclude other sleep disorders
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or asymmetric sensory or motor deficits suggesting a neuropathy or radiculopathy rather than primary RLS
Augmentation on dopaminergic therapy with earlier, more intense, and spreading symptoms
Symptoms secondary to unrecognised chronic kidney disease or severe iron deficiency
Severe sleep deprivation with significant mood disturbance or impaired daytime function
reference.prognosis: Primary restless legs syndrome is usually a chronic condition that can fluctuate over time, often worsening with age. Secondary forms may resolve when the underlying cause, such as iron deficiency or pregnancy, is corrected. Most patients achieve good symptom control with appropriate treatment, though augmentation can complicate long-term dopaminergic therapy.
pitfalls: Failing to check and correct iron status, missing a readily treatable driver of symptoms
Overlooking culprit medications that provoke or worsen the syndrome
Relying on long-term dopamine agonists and precipitating augmentation
Confusing the condition with akathisia, cramps, or neuropathy and treating the wrong problem
management: Check iron status and replace iron with oral or intravenous supplementation when ferritin or transferrin saturation is low, even with a normal haemoglobin
Review and withdraw aggravating drugs where possible, including many antidepressants, sedating antihistamines and dopamine antagonists
Advise sleep hygiene and reduced caffeine and alcohol intake as first-line non-pharmacological measures
For troublesome symptoms start an alpha-2-delta ligand such as gabapentin or pregabalin, often preferred to limit augmentation
Use a dopamine agonist such as pramipexole, ropinirole or rotigotine with caution, monitoring for augmentation and impulse-control disorders
Treat secondary contributors including uraemia and pregnancy-related symptoms
Reserve low-potency opioids for refractory cases or dopaminergic augmentation under specialist supervision
